items.title: [virtualenv] virtualenv: Builtin creation follows linked environment directories
items.summary: SummaryThe builtin creator accepts existing directory symlinks through ensure_dir() and writes environment files through thosedirectories. This permits writes outside the requested destination.Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this as ANT-2026-MUFJEG11 in virtualenv-20261015-005, received on 15 October 2026.Affected areaDirectory preparation before environment files are created.Attacker-controlled inputAnother account must be able to prepare linked entries below the chosen destination before creation. The invoking usermust have access to the linked destination. This does not require write access to the target itself under the otheraccount.Affected codeThe relevant 21.14.8 source is inbuiltin creator,ensure_dir().MechanismThe builtin creator calls ensure_dir() for bin, lib, and package directories. ensure_dir() accepts an existingsymlink to a directory because exists() follows it. Interpreter creation, seed installation, and activation-scriptgeneration then write through that parent link. A final-file check cannot prevent a write through a linked parent.--clear removes the planted tree first; ordinary creation over a prepared destination reaches it.Reproduction and evidenceThe scanner's project tree contains venv/bin -> ../../.local/bin and a .pth file in the environment's package tree.With the user's initially empty ~/.local/bin first on PATH, virtualenv venv exited successfully and wrotepython*, pip*, and activate* into ~/.local/bin. The marker was absent immediately after creation; a laterpip --version on the user's PATH loaded the seeded environment and the planted .pth code wrote the marker. Asecond case began with the bin link resolving inside the environment; replacement of a planted package link duringseeding changed where it resolved, and writes again reached ~/.local/bin.The attacker must prepare entries in an existing destination. The .pth content is already attacker-controlled andwould run if the user used that environment directly; the added effect is creation-time writing or replacement outsidethe requested tree and an executable on the user's PATH pointing at it. The scanner traces this default builtin pathto 20.0.0b1. PR #3429 replaces linked directory components beforecreation. Concurrent parent replacement remains a separate case.Attack sequencesequenceDiagram    participant A as Prepared destination    participant V as Builtin creator    participant L as venv/bin symlink    participant H as ~/.local/bin    participant U as User    A->>L: point to ../../.local/bin    V->>L: ensure_dir accepts existing directory link    V->>H: write python, pip and activate files through link    V-->>U: creation reports success    U->>H: run pip found on PATH    H->>A: interpreter loads planted .pth    A-->>U: marker createdReproducer filesThe following files are from the scanner report for ANT-2026-MUFJEG11. They were tested against commit a857a7823c73in the scanner image. The repro entrypoint expects companion files under /tmp/repro.d; cases that change user IDsneed a disposable root-capable container. The last output line is BUG when the reported behavior occurs. These filesare included as evidence and were not rerun for this advisory update.repro#!/usr/bin/env python3import osimport shutilimport subprocessimport sysfrom pathlib import PathWORK = Path("/tmp/planted-bin-link")shutil.rmtree(WORK, ignore_errors=True)def user_creates_venv_in_checkout_then_runs_pip(home, make_checkout):    local_bin = home / ".local/bin"    user_env = {"HOME": str(home), "PATH": f"{local_bin}:{os.environ['PATH']}"}    local_bin_before = set(os.listdir(local_bin))    payload_marker = home / "PWNED"    # the attacker's checkout arrives at ~/project    subprocess.run([sys.executable, f"/tmp/repro.d/{make_checkout}", home / "project"], check=True)    venv = home / "project/venv"    print(f"CONTROL  venv/bin before the run resolves to {os.path.realpath(venv / 'bin')}")    # default options; the flag only keeps the run off the network    subprocess.run(["virtualenv", "--no-periodic-update", "--quiet", "venv"], cwd=home / "project", env=user_env, check=True)    written = sorted(set(os.listdir(local_bin)) - local_bin_before)    payload_ran_at_creation = payload_marker.exists()    print(f"OBSERVED venv/bin after the run resolves to  {os.path.realpath(venv / 'bin')}")    print(f"OBSERVED virtualenv wrote to {local_bin}: {written}")    print(f"OBSERVED ~/PWNED exists after virtualenv: {payload_ran_at_creation}")    # later, in another folder, the user runs pip    pip = subprocess.run(["pip", "--version"], cwd=home, env=user_env, capture_output=True, text=True)    print(f"OBSERVED pip --version: {(pip.stdout + pip.stderr).strip()}")    print(f"OBSERVED ~/PWNED exists after pip: {payload_marker.exists()}")    return written, payload_marker.exists() and not payload_ran_at_creationprint("--- checkout_with_bin_link.py: venv/bin -> ../../.local/bin")home = WORK / "bin-link"(home / ".local/bin").mkdir(parents=True)written_1, pip_ran_payload_1 =

items.title: [virtualenv] virtualenv: Deletion recovery can change a symlink target's mode
items.summary: SummaryThe deletion error handler obtains permission bits with lstat() but applies them through chmod(), which followssymlinks. On an eligible unlink failure this can change permissions outside the destination.Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this as ANT-2026-UK90QC27 in virtualenv-20261015-005, received on 15 October 2026.Affected areaPermission recovery after a filesystem deletion error.Attacker-controlled inputA deletion must fail on a symbolic-link entry and enter the permission-recovery branch. The invoking user must havepermission to change the target mode. This is conditional error handling, not the normal successful unlink path.Affected codeThe relevant 21.14.8 source is insafe_delete().Mechanismsafe_delete() asks shutil.rmtree() to retry a failed removal after adding owner-write permission. Its error handlercalls os.lstat(path) for mode bits but os.chmod(path, ...) to apply them. For a symlink, lstat reads the link'smode while chmod follows the link. A link inside a read-only directory can therefore cause the target's mode to become0777 before the retry fails. The target must be owned by the invoking user and initially not writable by that user;root does not reach this failure path.Reproduction and evidenceThe scanner packed a project containing a mode-0555 venv/bin/python/ directory and a symlink inside it pointing tothe user's mode-0400 keys/deploy.pem. An unprivileged user unpacked it and ran both plain virtualenv venv andvirtualenv --clear venv. Both commands exited with PermissionError naming the directory inside venv, while thekey's mode changed from 0400 to 0777. A control archive with a writable directory completed normally and left thekey at 0400. The read-only mode survives tar or cp -a; a normal git clone does not preserve this setup.This changes permissions; it does not read the target or complete the virtualenv operation. Another account can use thewidened mode only if it can traverse the target's parent directories. The scanner dates the active error handler to#3222, first released in 21.7.5. PR #3427 avoids POSIX mode changes ondeletion failure and handles Windows read-only entries without following reparse points.Attack sequencesequenceDiagram    participant A as Prepared read-only venv tree    participant V as safe_delete error handler    participant L as Symlink in venv    participant K as User's 0400 key    A->>V: virtualenv venv or --clear venv    V->>L: unlink fails in 0555 directory    V->>L: lstat returns link mode 0777    V->>L: chmod follows symlink    L->>K: target mode becomes 0777    V-->>A: retry fails with PermissionError    Note over K: Other accounts can use new mode if parent paths are traversableReproducer filesThe following files are from the scanner report for ANT-2026-UK90QC27. They were tested against commit a857a7823c73in the scanner image. The repro entrypoint expects companion files under /tmp/repro.d; cases that change user IDsneed a disposable root-capable container. The last output line is BUG when the reported behavior occurs. These filesare included as evidence and were not rerun for this advisory update.repro#!/usr/bin/env python3import osimport statimport subprocessimport sysimport tempfilefrom pathlib import PathNOBODY = 65534work = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="repro-safe-delete-"))os.chmod(work, 0o755)os.chown(work, NOBODY, NOBODY)# the attacker's project archive (venv/bin/python read-only), and the same archive with that folder writablemake_archive = [sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/make_project_archive.py"]subprocess.run([*make_archive, work / "read-only.tar", "555"], check=True)subprocess.run([*make_archive, work / "writable.tar", "755"], check=True)subprocess.run(["tar", "-tvf", work / "read-only.tar"], check=True)# from here on an ordinary user: root's unlink never fails, so safe_delete's error handler would never runos.setgroups([])os.setgid(NOBODY)os.setuid(NOBODY)os.umask(0o022)def unpack_next_to_key_and_run_virtualenv(label, home_name, archive_name, *options):    home = work / home_name    archive = work / archive_name    key = home / "keys" / "deploy.pem"    key.parent.mkdir(parents=True)    key.write_text("PRIVATE KEY\n")    key.chmod(0o400)    subprocess.run(["tar", "-xf", archive], cwd=home, check=True)    mode_before = stat.S_IMODE(key.stat().st_mode)    command = ["virtualenv", "--no-periodic-update", "-q", *options, "venv"]    # HOME is where virtualenv keeps its app-data; nobody's own, /nonexistent, cannot hold it    result = subprocess.run(        command,        cwd=home / "proj",        env={**os.environ, "HOME": str(home)},        stdout=subprocess.PIPE,        stderr=subprocess.STDOUT,        text=True,    )    mode_after = stat.S_IMODE(key.stat().st_mode)    print(f"{label} {archive_name}, `{' '.join(command)}`: exit {result.returncode} {result.stdout.strip()}")    print(f"{label} {key} mode {mode_before:#o} -> {mode_after:#o}")    return mode_before, mode_aftercontrol = unpack_next_to_key_and_run_virtualenv("CONTROL ", "home-c

items.title: [virtualenv] virtualenv: Generated POSIX console launchers interpret destination paths as shell syntax
items.summary: SummaryA destination path supplied to virtualenv can be interpreted as shell syntax by a generated POSIX console launcher. Theapp-data seeder and pip delegate launcher generation to distlib but supply the interpreter path in a form that does notpreserve it as literal data in the shell wrapper.Affected areaPOSIX console scripts generated by the app-data seeder or pip when the interpreter path requires a shell wrapper.Windows executable launchers are not affected by this path.Attacker-controlled inputAn attacker must influence the environment destination passed to virtualenv, and the user must subsequently run agenerated launcher. The attacker does not need to modify an installed executable or control the user's app-data cache.Affected codeThe relevant 21.14.8 source is inScriptMakerCustom.MechanismThe app-data seeder passes the environment's interpreter path through enquote_executable() to distlib's ScriptMaker.It adds double quotes for a path with a space but does not escape shell expansions inside those quotes. When the pathhas a space or the shebang exceeds 127 bytes, distlib emits a #!/bin/sh wrapper with a line shaped like'''exec' "<path>" "$0" "$@". The shell expands $(...) and backticks in that path when the launcher is run. The samewrapper must also parse as Python, which exposes additional quote and backslash cases. Environment creation andactivation do not trigger the shell payload.Reproduction and evidenceThe scanner created three environments: a control under my -touch PWNED- project, one undermy $(touch PWNED) project, and one under a path of more than 127 bytes ending in $(touch${IFS}PWNED). Each wascreated without producing PWNED. Running the generated bin/pip --version created PWNED in both attack cases; thecontrol created none. The long-path case reached the shell wrapper without a space. This reproduces execution by thegenerated launcher, with the user's privileges, rather than during seeding.The report dates the app-data seeder's distlib launcher integration to #1579, first released in 20.0.2.PR #3417 quotes the raw interpreter path for the POSIX wrapper andrepairs launchers written by the pip seeder. Pip's own distlib can write a vulnerable wrapper again during a later pipinstall or upgrade; the proposed virtualenv fix does not change pip's vendored code. The maintainer-provided follow-upreview reports that later path separately.Attack sequencesequenceDiagram    participant A as Destination supplier    participant V as virtualenv seeder    participant D as distlib ScriptMaker    participant S as Generated bin/pip    participant U as User    A->>V: path contains $(touch PWNED)    V->>D: pass interpreter path with incomplete shell quoting    D->>S: write /bin/sh wrapper    Note over V,S: no payload runs during creation or activation    U->>S: pip --version    S->>S: shell expands path and runs touch    S-->>U: PWNED appears with user's privilegesReproducer filesThe following files are from the scanner report for ANT-2026-5DZVLGL1. They were tested against commit a857a7823c73in the scanner image. The repro entrypoint expects companion files under /tmp/repro.d; cases that change user IDsneed a disposable root-capable container. The last output line is BUG when the reported behavior occurs. These filesare included as evidence and were not rerun for this advisory update.repro#!/usr/bin/env python3import shutilimport subprocessfrom pathlib import PathWORK = Path("/tmp/repro-console-script")# The attacker's whole input: the name of a directory above the environment (a repository, a project folder).DIRECTORY_NAMES = {    "CONTROL": "my -touch PWNED- project",    "OBSERVED": "my $(touch PWNED) project",    # no space: distlib also picks the /bin/sh launcher once "#!<dest>/bin/python" is longer than 127 bytes    "OBSERVED_LONG": "p" * 120 + "$(touch${IFS}PWNED)",}shutil.rmtree(WORK, ignore_errors=True)pip_printed = {}created_by_pip = {}for label, name in DIRECTORY_NAMES.items():    # the payload can hold no "/", so it touches a relative PWNED: each case gets its own empty working directory    cwd = WORK / label / "cwd"    venv = WORK / label / name / "venv"    cwd.mkdir(parents=True)    # set up: the user creates an environment there with default options (--no-periodic-update keeps it offline)    subprocess.run(["virtualenv", "--quiet", "--no-periodic-update", str(venv)], cwd=cwd, check=True)    assert list(cwd.iterdir()) == [], "environment creation must not have created anything"    # trigger: the user runs the seeded pip; argv is a list, so the only shell that reads the name is bin/pip's own    pip = subprocess.run([venv / "bin" / "pip", "--version"], cwd=cwd, capture_output=True, text=True)    pip_printed[label] = pip.stdout    created_by_pip[label] = sorted(p.name for p in cwd.iterdir())    launcher = (venv / "bin" / "pip").read_text().splitlines()    print(f"{label}: directory name {name!r}")    print(f"  bin/pip line 1: {launcher[0]}")    print(f"  bin/pip line 2: {launcher[1]}")    print(f"

items.title: [Pillow]  Pillow: Memory disclosure and segfault in libtiff encoder via crafted TIFF tags
items.summary: ============================================================================Memory disclosure and segfault in libtiff encoder via crafted TIFF tagsLocation: src/encode.c:1014  in PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew()Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6============================================================================A crafted TIFF file of a few hundred bytes makes Pillow copy an attacker-chosen amount of its own process memory into the TIFF it writes back out, or crash the process outright. The trigger is an ordinary Image.open() followed by a bare im.save(fp, "TIFF"). The only precondition is that the application re-saves images as TIFF. When the uploaded file is compressed, Pillow routes that save through libtiff automatically, with no options from the application. The attached reproducer does this with a 356-byte LZW TIFF: one crafted tag comes back holding 65536 bytes taken from _imaging.so's read-only data, and a second crafted tag makes the worker die with SIGSEGV on every run.The bug is in PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew (src/encode.c). It decides what arguments to pass to the variadic TIFFSetField() from the shape of the Python value (scalar, tuple or bytes). It assumes its ImagingLibTiffMergeFieldInfo() call defined how libtiff will read them. But TIFFMergeFieldInfo() never overrides libtiff's built-in field table, so libtiff reads the arguments according to its own definition of the tag:For a counted array tag such as DNGPrivateData (50740), a count-1 integer in the source file is taken as the byte count. The data pointer is then read from an argument slot Pillow never wrote, and that many bytes are copied into the output.For a fixed-size array tag such as ActiveArea (50829), the integer itself is used as the source address.Where that unwritten slot points depends on the compiler. In the tested clang build it points into _imaging.so, and a larger count returned thousands of pointers into libpython, libc and libtiff, which defeats address-space randomisation for anyone chaining another bug. When the application preserves metadata with tiffinfo=im.tag_v2, a 64-bit entry turns ActiveArea into a 16-byte read from an address the attacker chooses. All observed memory errors are reads; no out-of-bounds write was found.Other branches of the same loop share the defect and are reachable from crafted TIFFs or from EXIF in JPEG/PNG/WebP re-saved as compressed TIFF. These are the bytes, RATIONAL-tuple and typed-tuple branches, and a BYTE-typed ColorMap. The file-reachable forwarding was introduced in a3d45e9cefd0 ("Added custom int and float TIFF tags") and first released in 5.4.0.DetailsPyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew (src/encode.c:777-1060) chooses the argumentlist it hands to the variadic TIFFSetField() from the Python value of eachtag — scalar vs. tuple vs. bytes, and a type that is either autodetected orcopied from the source file's IFD — and assumes that its ownImagingLibTiffMergeFieldInfo() registration defines how libtiff will read theva_list. It does not: libtiff keeps its built-in definition for every tag italready knows, and core tags are never registered at all. libtiff thereforeconsumes the varargs as (count, pointer), (pointer) or three pointersaccording to its field table, whatever Pillow actually pushed. The encodernever consults that table (TIFFFindField / TIFFFieldPassCount /TIFFFieldWriteCount / TIFFFieldDataType) before the call.The most severe instance, and the one the attached reproducer exercises: when aTIFF is re-saved through the libtiff writer, every tag of the source IFD thatPillow does not recognise is forwarded to libtiff with TIFFSetField(). Acount-1 integer entry is passed as a single scalar vararg. If libtiff's ownfield table defines that tag number as an array field, libtiff consumes thevarargs as (count, pointer) or (pointer) instead, so the attacker's integerbecomes either the number of bytes to copy from a never-written vararg slot, orthe source address itself. The same mismatch is reachable through the typedtuple branches (tuple length consumed as a pointer for fixed-count built-intags such as CFARepeatPatternDim, even when the source file is well-formed),the bytes, TIFF_RATIONAL-tuple and core-tag branches of the same loop;those are listedunder Other branches with the same defect below and need to be covered by thesame fix.A 181-byte TIFF (16×16 RGB, one LZW strip, plus one extra IFD entry50740 / LONG / count 1 / value 4096 — DNGPrivateData) opened withImage.open() and saved with a bare im.save(buf, "TIFF") produces a 4296-byteoutput whose tag 50740 holds 4096 bytes that occur nowhere in the input; scanning/proc/self/mem finds them in the read-only data segment of _imaging.so.Changing the extra entry to 50829 / LONG / 1 / 64 (ActiveArea) makes the sametwo calls segfault in memcpy(dst, src=0x40, n=16) underImagingLibTiffSetField ← PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew. An ASan build of theextensions reports READ of size 4096 in memcpy called fromsrc/encode.c:1014 for the firs

items.title: [Pillow] Pillow: Heap buffer overflow in _tiffWriteProc when saving TIFF to BytesIO
items.summary: ============================================================================Heap buffer overflow in _tiffWriteProc when saving TIFF to BytesIOLocation: src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:94  in _tiffWriteProc()Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6============================================================================Pillow can write attacker-chosen data past the end of a heap buffer when it saves a TIFF image to an in-memory destination such as io.BytesIO rather than to a file. The same code also copies leftover heap memory from the process into the saved file. Anyone who can supply an image to a service that opens it and re-saves it as TIFF this way can trigger this with default settings. The attached reproducer crashes the process, and the overflow could potentially be developed further, but code execution is not demonstrated here.The bug is in _tiffWriteProc in src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c. This is the write callback for the in-memory sink that Pillow gives libtiff whenever the save target has no fileno(). While writing the directory, libtiff seeks past the current end of data and writes tag values there. _tiffWriteProc sizes its realloc() from state->size + size instead of from the write position state->loc. As a result, the first out-of-line tag value written after that seek can run past the allocation by up to the size of the directory: 12 bytes per entry, 126 bytes in the minimal case, and 2384 bytes observed with a 331-entry directory. The overflowing bytes are the tail of a tag value taken from the uploaded file.No save options are needed, because compression and tags are inherited from the source image. The overflow does require an attacker-sized out-of-line tag to reach libtiff. That happens when the opened TIFF is saved directly (ImageDescription, DocumentName or XMP), or through an embedded ICC profile, which survives copy() in im.info. The bytes libtiff skips for alignment are never initialised, so any compressed TIFF over 64 KiB written this way also leaks one stale heap byte per padding hole. That leak needs no crafted tag.The attached reproducer builds a 131 KB PackBits TIFF and runs Image.open(...).save(io.BytesIO(), "TIFF"). Saving the same image to a file path succeeds, but the BytesIO save aborts with glibc's malloc(): corrupted top size. A second part of the script shows uninitialised heap bytes at the padding offsets of a BytesIO save that are zero in the file save. Saves to real files are unaffected. The defect dates to e782fe721e01 (2013) and has been present since Pillow 2.0.0.DetailsWhen im.save() writes a TIFF through libtiff to a target that has no usable fileno() (io.BytesIO, an HTTP response object, a storage backend stream), libtiff is opened with TIFFClientOpen() on Pillow's own in-memory sink, _tiffWriteProc / _tiffSeekProc in src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c. libtiff treats that sink like a file: when it writes the directory it seeks beyond the current end of data (to eof + IFD size, where the out-of-line tag values go, and one byte further after every odd-length tag value to keep offsets even) and writes there. On a real file the kernel grows the file and zero-fills the gap. The memory sink does neither correctly:_tiffWriteProc sizes its realloc() from state->size + size instead of state->loc + size, so the first write after such a seek can land past the end of the new allocation — a heap buffer overflow whose content is tag data taken from the image being saved.The bytes that libtiff skips are never written, and the grown region is a bare realloc(), so they reach the output TIFF with whatever the heap held before.Both are reachable with default settings by the ordinary "re-encode the upload" sequence Image.open(upload); im.save(io.BytesIO(), "TIFF") with no save options: compression defaults to the source file's (src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1734), any compression other than raw selects the libtiff writer (:1746), the source's tag_v2 entries are passed through to libtiff (:1959), and a target without fileno() leaves _fp = 0 (:1928-1935), i.e. the memory sink. The overflow half additionally needs an attacker-controlled out-of-line tag value of the right length to reach libtiff. With the opened TiffImageFile saved directly (tag_v2 passthrough) that can be a ~64 KiB ASCII tag (269/270/271/272) or the XMP packet (tag 700, type BYTE — arbitrary bytes), and the number of tags the upload carries sets the IFD size, i.e. the overrun length (12 bytes per entry; 2384 bytes with a 331-entry IFD observed). After convert()/resize()/thumbnail()/copy() the tag_v2 entries are gone, but im.info["compression"] (still selecting libtiff) and im.info["icc_profile"] survive and the ICC profile is written as tag 34675 (:1822-1824), an equally attacker-controlled out-of-line value: Image.open(x).copy().save(BytesIO(), "TIFF") with the payload in the ICC profile produces the identical ASan report. The stale-byte half needs no attacker tag at all.Proof (overflow). A 131 198-byte hand-built TIFF

items.title: [pillow] Pillow: Heap use-after-free when encoding TIFF to an in-memory buffer
items.summary: SummarySaving an image as TIFF to an in-memory buffer can trigger a heap use-after-free if libtiff rejects a tag at encode time. When TIFFWriteScanline fails, the encoder frees its output buffer but leaves the libtiff handle open. Later, when the encoder object is torn down, TIFFClose flushes buffered bytes through the write callback and writes into the freed buffer. An application that re-encodes attacker-influenced images to TIFF in memory can be crashed and is a candidate for remote code execution.DetailsThe failure path in ImagingLibTiffEncode frees clientstate->data for the in-memory case but does not close the TIFF or null clientstate->tiff (the file-descriptor branch just above it does set tiff = NULL):src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1041-1046Teardown then calls ImagingLibTiffEncodeCleanup, which runs TIFFClose(tiff) because tiff is still set:src/encode.c:99-101src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:955TIFFClose flushes through _tiffWriteProc, which reallocs and memcpys into the freed state->data:src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:103-115The Predictor tag is a convenient trigger: the floating-point predictor (value 3) is invalid for integer sample data, so libtiff aborts the write.PoCimport iofrom PIL import Image# In-memory TIFF re-encode. libtiff rejects Predictor=3 (floating point) on integer# data, so TIFFWriteScanline fails. The encoder frees clientstate->data but leaves the# TIFF open; cleanup's TIFFClose then writes through the callback into the freed buffer.im = Image.new("L", (64, 64))buf = io.BytesIO()im.save(buf, format="TIFF", compression="tiff_lzw", tiffinfo={317: 3})  # 317 = PredictorRun it:$ python 01_poc.pyPredictorSetup: Floating point "Predictor" not supported with 1 data format.OSError: encoder error -2 when writing image fileSegmentation fault (core dumped)Observed on a source build of commit 3e2ab96 with libtiff. The process aborts during cleanup after the encoder error. Depending on heap state the same run sometimes reports corrupted double-linked list instead of a segfault; both are the same write into freed memory.Under AddressSanitizer (build with -fsanitize=address), relevant frames:==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free on address 0x7ef737b48804WRITE of size 4 at 0x7ef737b48804 thread T0    #1 _tiffWriteProc                 src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:115    #3 TIFFFlush                      libtiff.so.6    #5 TIFFClose                      libtiff.so.6    #6 ImagingLibTiffEncodeCleanup    src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:955    #7 _dealloc                       src/encode.c:100freed by thread T0 here:    #1 ImagingLibTiffEncode           src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1045    #2 _encode                        src/encode.c:139previously allocated by thread T0 here:    #1 ImagingLibTiffEncodeInit       src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:863    #2 PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew    src/encode.c:757SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:115 in _tiffWriteProcThe buffer allocated in ImagingLibTiffEncodeInit is freed in ImagingLibTiffEncode, then written by _tiffWriteProc during the TIFFClose flush that runs from the encoder's _dealloc.ImpactUse-after-free in a C extension. Affects any service that converts or thumbnails untrusted images to TIFF in memory (a BytesIO or other non-seekable target). Result is a crash and possible memory corruption leading to code execution.Referenceshttps://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/security/advisories/GHSA-4rr5-89j8-mwwmhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-112396https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/commit/dc95da20207827a062cfbf551ee9f6031465a8bbhttps://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/releases/tag/13.0.0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4rr5-89j8-mwwm

items.title: [Pillow] Pillow: Infinite loop in PdfParser.rewrite_pages on page tree Parent cycle
items.summary: ============================================================================Infinite loop in PdfParser.rewrite_pages on page tree Parent cycleLocation: src/PIL/PdfParser.py:505  in PdfParser.rewrite_pages()Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6============================================================================A PDF file of a few hundred bytes makes Pillow hang forever, holding one processor core at 100%, when an application tries to append an image to it. Anyone who can supply the existing PDF to an application that calls im.save(fp, "PDF", append=True) (or save_all=True, append=True) can tie up that worker indefinitely. Memory use stays flat, so only an external timeout stops it.The bug is in PdfParser.rewrite_pages() in src/PIL/PdfParser.py (the while pages_tree_node_ref: loop at line 505). For each original page, it walks the /Parent chain upward and stops only when it reaches a node with no /Parent. It keeps no record of nodes it has already visited, so a loop in that chain never ends. The simplest case is a /Pages root that lists itself as its own /Parent; a longer cycle among page-tree nodes behaves the same way. The path is PdfImagePlugin._save() → write_catalog() → rewrite_pages(), and it is reached whether the save target is a file path or a BytesIO. Plain Image.open() pipelines are not affected, because Pillow only parses PDFs on the append path.This is a sibling of CVE-2026-42310 (the cyclic trailer /Prev loop in the same parser). The processed_offsets guard added to read_prev_trailer() for that issue does not cover this walk. The loop was introduced in 24ecfe315ab5 (2018-03-03) and has been present in every release since 5.1.0.The attached reproducer builds two in-memory PDFs and appends a 4×4 image to each. The normal file finishes in about 45 ms. The 333-byte self-parented file is still spinning inside rewrite_pages() when a 5-second watchdog interrupts it. Two alternative fixes are attached: one silently tolerates the cycle, and one rejects the file with an error.DetailsPdfParser.rewrite_pages() walks the /Parent chain of every pre-existing page upward and stops only when a node has no /Parent. It keeps no record of visited nodes, so a page-tree node whose /Parent points at itself, or at any node below it, makes the walk spin forever.The following 333-byte file is a valid one-page PDF except that object 2, the page-tree root, declares /Parent 2 0 R:%PDF-1.41 0 obj<</Type /Catalog /Pages 2 0 R>>endobj2 0 obj<</Type /Pages /Kids [3 0 R] /Count 1 /Parent 2 0 R>>endobj3 0 obj<</Type /Page /Parent 2 0 R /MediaBox [0 0 10 10]>>endobjxref0 40000000000 65535 f 0000000009 00000 n 0000000056 00000 n 0000000125 00000 n trailer<</Size 4 /Root 1 0 R>>startxref192%%EOFImage.new("RGB", (4, 4)).save(io.BytesIO(pdf), "PDF", append=True) on these bytes never returns and holds one core at 100 % (the same happens when the target is a file path opened r+b). Interrupting it with SIGALRM after 5 s gives this traceback every time:  File "src/PIL/PdfImagePlugin.py", line 263, in _save    existing_pdf.write_catalog()  File "src/PIL/PdfParser.py", line 473, in write_catalog    self.rewrite_pages()  File "src/PIL/PdfParser.py", line 505, in rewrite_pages    while pages_tree_node_ref:The same file without /Parent 2 0 R on object 2 is appended to in ~30 ms.The loop:# src/PIL/PdfParser.py:483-510def rewrite_pages(self) -> None:    pages_tree_nodes_to_delete = []    for i, page_ref in enumerate(self.orig_pages):        page_info = self.cached_objects[page_ref]        del self.xref_table[page_ref.object_id]        pages_tree_nodes_to_delete.append(page_info[PdfName(b"Parent")])        …    # delete redundant Pages tree nodes from xref table    for pages_tree_node_ref in pages_tree_nodes_to_delete:        while pages_tree_node_ref:            pages_tree_node = self.cached_objects[pages_tree_node_ref]            if pages_tree_node_ref.object_id in self.xref_table:                del self.xref_table[pages_tree_node_ref.object_id]            pages_tree_node_ref = pages_tree_node.get(b"Parent", None)    self.orig_pages = []How the input gets there: with append=True, PdfImagePlugin._save() opens the existing bytes with PdfParser.PdfParser(f=fp, …, mode="r+b") (src/PIL/PdfImagePlugin.py:199), whose constructor calls read_pdf_info(). That reads the catalog, reads the page-tree root through read_indirect() — which stores every object it reads in self.cached_objects (src/PIL/PdfParser.py:1077) — and flattens the tree with linearize_page_tree(), which read_indirect()s every /Kids entry. So after parsing, orig_pages == [3 0 R] and objects 2 and 3 are both in cached_objects. _save() then calls existing_pdf.write_catalog() → rewrite_pages().For the file above, the first loop puts page 3's /Parent, 2 0 R, into pages_tree_nodes_to_delete. The inner while looks object 2 up in cached_objects, removes it from the xref table on the first pass, and sets pages_tree_node_ref to object 2's /Parent — which is 2 0 R again. Nothin

items.title: [Pillow] Pillow: APNG background disposal allocates full canvas before decompression bomb check
items.summary: ============================================================================APNG background disposal allocates full canvas before decompression bomb checkLocation: src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py:1000  in PngImageFile._seek()Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6============================================================================A 126-byte animated PNG file makes Pillow's Image.open() allocate and fill memory sized by the image dimensions the file claims, before Pillow's built-in check for oversized images runs. A file claiming 22000×22000 pixels costs about 1.9 GB. Anyone who can get an application to open an image they supply, with default settings and no further calls such as load(), can cause a multi-gigabyte memory spike per file. If the claimed size exceeds the machine's free memory, the operating system kills the process outright.The bug is in PngImageFile._seek() in src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py (around line 1000). For any APNG, _open() calls self._seek(0). When the first fcTL chunk requests OP_BACKGROUND disposal, _seek() calls Image.core.fill(self.mode, self.size) with the full IHDR size, which allocates and zero-fills width×height×4 bytes. OP_PREVIOUS takes the same path, because frame 0 rewrites it to OP_BACKGROUND. This all happens inside the plugin factory, so Image.open()'s _decompression_bomb_check(im.size) only runs after the memory has been touched. A 1×1 frame rectangle passes the only checks on the way.Below available memory, the allocation is freed when DecompressionBombError propagates, so sustained pressure needs repeated or concurrent uploads. A 45000×45000 header gets the process killed by the out-of-memory killer on an 8 GB host. The attached reproducer opens two such files that differ in one byte (dispose_op 0 vs 1). Both end in DecompressionBombError, but peak resident memory is 17 MB for the first and 1864 MB for the second. The eager fill was introduced in 5e4e0fa6ee67 ("Use disposal settings from previous frame", December 2020) and first shipped in 8.1.0. Two candidate patches with a regression test are attached.DetailsFor an APNG whose first fcTL chunk requests OP_BACKGROUND disposal, PngImageFile._open() creates and zero-fills a core image of the full IHDR-declared size. This happens inside the plugin factory, i.e. before Image.open() gets to _decompression_bomb_check(im.size), so the check that is meant to reject oversized headers without allocating anything runs only after the allocation has been made and touched.The following 126-byte file (all chunk lengths and CRCs valid) makes Image.open(io.BytesIO(data)), with default MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS and no load(), reach 1.86 GB resident (ru_maxrss) and then raise DecompressionBombError. The byte-identical file with dispose_op=0 raises the same error at 17 MB.IHDR  width=22000 height=22000 bit_depth=8 colour_type=6 (RGBA)acTL  num_frames=2 num_plays=0fcTL  seq=0 w=1 h=1 x=0 y=0 delay=1/10 dispose_op=1 (OP_BACKGROUND) blend_op=0IDAT  zlib(00 00 00 00 00)                      # one 1x1 RGBA scanlineIENDWith width=height=45000 (8.1 GB canvas) the same call attempts the full allocation: under a 4 GiB RLIMIT_AS it fails with MemoryError from the allocator instead of DecompressionBombError; without a cap, on an 8 GB host with no swap, the process is OOM-killed.Code pathImage.open() runs the bomb check only after the plugin's constructor (and therefore _open()) has returned:# src/PIL/Image.py:3699-3701                    im = factory(fp, filename)                    _decompression_bomb_check(im.size)                    return imFor a plain PNG that ordering is fine: PngImageFile._open() only parses chunks up to the first IDAT and records self._size from IHDR; nothing is allocated from it. For an APNG (acTL seen, so im_n_frames is set) _open() additionally positions on frame 0:# src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py:845-853        if self.png.im_n_frames is not None:            …            self._seek(0)_seek(0) copies disposal and bbox from the fcTL chunk into self.dispose_op / self.dispose_extent and then prepares the disposal image for the next frame eagerly, using the full image size:# src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py:991-1001        if self._prev_im is None and self.dispose_op == Disposal.OP_PREVIOUS:            self.dispose_op = Disposal.OP_BACKGROUND        self.dispose = None        if self.dispose_op == Disposal.OP_PREVIOUS:            …        elif self.dispose_op == Disposal.OP_BACKGROUND:            self.dispose = Image.core.fill(self.mode, self.size)            self.dispose = self._crop(self.dispose, self.dispose_extent)Image.core.fill is _fill() in src/_imaging.c:711, which does ImagingNewDirty(mode, xsize, ysize) followed by ImagingFill(); ImagingFill (src/libImaging/Fill.c:23) writes every row, so the whole width*height*4 bytes become resident rather than merely reserved. self.size here is the IHDR size (22000×22000), not the 1×1 frame rectangle. The _crop on the next line does call _decompression_bomb_check, but on the fcTL rectangle

items.title: [pillow] Pillow: MSP RLE decoder expands a tiny file into unbounded memory
items.summary: SummaryThe MSP RLE decoder expands run-length data into an in-memory buffer with no cap tied to the declared image size. A small file that passes the pixel-count check can force hundreds of megabytes or more of allocation when the application loads pixels.DetailsThe MSP decoder writes each run into an unbounded io.BytesIO and can expand roughly 85x per run:src/PIL/MspImagePlugin.py:144-146ImpactMemory-exhaustion denial of service from a tiny crafted image in any application that loads pixels. The expansion is decoupled from the declared pixel count, so MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS does not bound it.Referenceshttps://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/security/advisories/GHSA-gg2r-wvfm-q9rxhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-112892https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/commit/5dcb630b9798efd91929cb873d677aeee6ed0bb3https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/releases/tag/13.0.0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-gg2r-wvfm-q9rx

items.title: [Pillow] Pillow: Quadratic-time DoS in PDF save_all (PdfParser.next_object_id)
items.summary: ============================================================================Quadratic-time DoS in PDF save_all (PdfParser.next_object_id)Location: src/PIL/PdfParser.py:629  in next_object_id()Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6============================================================================Pillow's PDF writer takes time proportional to the square of the number of frames when it saves a multi-frame image as a multi-page PDF. Anyone who can get an application to convert their uploaded image this way can tie up a worker at full CPU for minutes with a small file. A 240 KB animated image takes about 70 seconds, a 720 KB one an estimated 10 minutes, and a 125-byte animated PNG that merely declares a large frame count triggers the same slowdown with no upper bound short of 2³¹ frames. Memory stays under 100 MB and the decompression-bomb limit never applies.The cause is PdfParser.next_object_id() in src/PIL/PdfParser.py, which finds the next free id by computing max(self.xref_table.keys()). XrefTable.keys() rebuilds three sets over every id reserved so far on each call. PdfImagePlugin._save() calls it three times (four for palette images with transparency) per frame, for n_frames frames, before any page is written. That makes the id-reservation loop alone O(N²). Because n_frames is taken from the file before any frame is seeked, APNG's acTL count drives the loop even when the frames don't exist. In that case the save raises OSError only after the full delay.The precondition is that the application calls im.save(..., "PDF", save_all=True) on the attacker's file; Image.open() and load() alone do not reach this code. The attached reproducer shows 4× the frames costing about 11× the CPU for a valid GIF and about 16× for a fixed 125-byte APNG. The behaviour was introduced in 6207b44ab1ff (2018-01-18) and first shipped in Pillow 5.1.0. A small patch that tracks the highest id in XrefTable makes the save linear.DetailsSaving a multi-frame image as a multi-page PDF (im.save(fp, "PDF", save_all=True)) costs CPU time proportional to the square of the frame count, independent of pixel content, because every object id the PDF writer reserves is found by rebuilding and scanning the set of all ids reserved so far.A 1×1-pixel animated GIF made of N identical 15-byte frames (built by the reproducer) gives, on a 2-CPU container with the stock build at this commit (absolute timings vary by machine; the growth rate does not):framesGIF sizeim.save(BytesIO(), "PDF", save_all=True)peak RSS2 00030 KB1.1 s8 000120 KB14.7 s16 000240 KB70 s60 MB32 000480 KB262 s95 MB48 000720 KBstill running at 120 s (extrapolated ≈ 10 min)Each doubling of the input roughly quadruples the time. cProfile of the 8 000-frame save attributes 13.5 s of 17.6 s to 24 003 calls of PdfParser.next_object_id (8.9 s inside XrefTable.keys, 3.9 s inside max); encoding and writing the 8 000 pages is the remaining ~4 s and scales linearly.The per-page id reservation loop runs before any page is written:# src/PIL/PdfImagePlugin.py:247-259  (_save)    for im in ims:        im_number_of_pages = 1        if save_all:            im_number_of_pages = getattr(im, "n_frames", 1)        …        for i in range(im_number_of_pages):            image_refs.append(existing_pdf.next_object_id(0))            if im.mode == "P" and "transparency" in im.info:                image_refs.append(existing_pdf.next_object_id(0))            page_refs.append(existing_pdf.next_object_id(0))            contents_refs.append(existing_pdf.next_object_id(0))n_frames comes straight from the file (for GIF it is the number of image blocks; the GIF plugin counts them by walking block headers, which is cheap). The frames do not even have to exist: the loop runs on n_frames before any frame is seeked, and for APNG n_frames is the num_frames value declared in the acTL chunk, rejected only if it is 0 or above 0x80000000 (src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py:716-720). A 125-byte APNG declaring 8 000 frames therefore costs the same ~10–13 s as the 120 KB GIF, and more without bound as the declared count grows. Each of the 3 (or 4, for P images with transparency) calls per frame lands here:# src/PIL/PdfParser.py:626-634    def next_object_id(self, offset: int | None = None) -> IndirectReference:        try:            # TODO: support reuse of deleted objects            reference = IndirectReference(max(self.xref_table.keys()) + 1, 0)        except ValueError:            reference = IndirectReference(1, 0)        if offset is not None:            self.xref_table[reference.object_id] = (offset, 0)        return reference# src/PIL/PdfParser.py:175-178  (XrefTable)    def keys(self) -> set[int]:        return (            set(self.existing_entries.keys()) - set(self.deleted_entries.keys())        ) | set(self.new_entries.keys())_save passes offset=0, so every reserved id is inserted into xref_table.new_entries. The k-th call therefore materialises three sets covering all k−1 previous ids, computes a diff

items.title: [Pillow] Pillow: PdfParser can recurse without limit in get_value() and linearize_page_tree()
items.summary:
SummaryPdfParser's get_value() can recurse without any limit and crash with an uncaught RecursionError. It is reachable through Image.save(im, fp=<pdf>, format="PDF", append=True) when the existing PDF file is attacker-controlled. This is the same class of bug as https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-r73j-pqj5-w3x7 (the /Prev trailer chain loop, fixed earlier this year), in the same file, but in two different functions that fix did not touch.Detailsget_value() in src/PIL/PdfParser.pyThis is a classmethod that takes max_nesting: int = -1 and has a guard:if max_nesting == 0:    return None, NoneEvery recursive call (nested arrays, dictionaries, indirect object definitions) passes max_nesting=max_nesting - 1. Since the default and every call site start at -1, this only ever counts down further negative: -1, -2, -3, and so on. It never equals exactly 0, so the guard never runs. A PDF object with a value nested a few thousand levels deep is enough to hit Python's recursion limit. It does not even need a valid /Pages tree, since read_pdf_info() parses the /Root object's own dictionary first, before checking anything else.This advisory reports a single vulnerability: an ineffective recursion-depth guard in PdfParser.get_value() (the sentinel  -1  default never reaches the == 0 check). The mention of GHSA-r73j-pqj5-w3x7 is comparative context for an already-fixed, already-CVE'd bug in a different function — it is not a second vulnerability being reported. The three trigger paths (nested arrays/dicts/indirect objects) are not independently fixable; they share one root cause and one fix location in  get_value() .Steps to reproduceBoth PDFs below are plain text, built directly in Python, no PDF library needed.from PIL.PdfParser import PdfParserdef build_pdf(root):    out = bytearray(b"%PDF-1.4
")    offset = len(out)    out += f"1 0 obj
".encode()    out += root    out += b"
endobj
"    out += b"xref
"    out += f"0 2
".encode()    out += b"0000000000 65535 f 
"    out += f"{offset:010d} 00000 ".encode() + b"n 
"    xref_offset = len(out)    out += b"xref
"    out += f"0 2
".encode()    out += b"0000000000 65535 f 
"    out += f"{offset:010d} 00000 ".encode() + b"n 
"    out += b"trailer
"    out += f"<< /Size 2 /Root 1 0 R >>
".encode()    out += b"startxref
"    out += f"{xref_offset}
".encode()    out += b"%%EOF"    return bytes(out)bomb = b"[" * 3000 + b"]" * 3000root = b"<< /Type /Catalog /Pages 2 0 R /Bomb " + bomb + b" >>"with open("nesting_bomb.pdf", "wb") as f:    f.write(build_pdf(root))PdfParser("nesting_bomb.pdf")     # raises RecursionErrorExpected: a clean PdfFormatError.Actual: raises a raw RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded.ImpactAvailability: an attacker who controls the content of a PDF file that an application later appends an image page to (Image.save(..., format="PDF", append=True)) can crash that request with a RecursionError, using a file of a few hundred bytes.Confidentiality: none.Integrity: none.Pillow cannot open PDFs for reading through Image.open(). PdfParser is only reached through the append-mode save path, so the app has to be doing that specific thing (for example, stamping or watermarking an existing PDF) for this to matter.Referenceshttps://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/security/advisories/GHSA-254f-3936-288hhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-112391https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/commit/94cb11c44ff7345414da17ebfea1598a529ad9cdhttps://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/releases/tag/13.0.0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-254f-3936-288h
